description: A broad cream-fleeced ewe lies flat in the straw while one lamb drives into her udder with its tail spinning like a propeller, its coat already dry and fluffed into tight curls, and its twin is still folded down beside her, coat in dark damp spikes, one outsized ear bent over at the tip.

A ewe stands square in her pen while two lambs work along her flank, both half-dry, damp and spiky at the belly, their backs barely clearing her knee, and a third has got its whole head through the hurdle gap and stands there, stumped, unable to work out how it happened.

A speckle-nosed ewe noses her twin lambs awake in the straw, one already lurching upright on legs too long for it and swaying, steam lifting visibly off its damp dark curls in the cold shed air, while the other keeps its chin hooked stubbornly over the bottom hurdle rail and refuses.

Three lambs press along a blocky black-faced ewe's flank, the nearest one a day old and bouncing all four feet off the straw at once for no reason, the other two still half-dry and folded close against her ribs, all three together taking up less of the pen than she does.

A ewe nudges her twin lambs apart to get at the straw beneath them, both lambs a few hours old and still damp and spiky at the belly, their tails going in unison while they feed, their backs barely level with her knee, a scrap of baler twine on the hurdle post gone furry from chewing.

A lamb drives into the bottle the shepherd holds with its whole body, both front feet leaving the straw, while its pen-mate shoulders hard into the shepherd's knee for its turn, the pair of them together not reaching the height of the hurdle's second rail, their tails spinning the whole time.

Two lambs flank the bottle the shepherd angles between them, each one braced with front feet spread and tail going flat out, their damp spiky bellies pressed against the shepherd's boots, a bootprint full of cloudy water in the pen gateway just behind.

A lamb shoulders its twin clean off the bottle propped against the hurdle post, claiming it entirely, both front feet off the ground, tail spinning, while the ousted twin stands with its nose against its sibling's flank and shoves, the pair of them barely clearing the bottom hurdle rail.

Two lambs stand in the one bright band of light coming through a gap in the shed boards, shoulder to shoulder, steam lifting steadily off their backs into the cold air above them, their tight curls lit sharp and clean, the rest of the pen dim and plain behind them.

Two lambs have found the one bright band laid right across the straw where the shed wall boards leave a gap, and stand in it pressed together with steam curling off their backs, while a third sits just off the edge of the bright patch with a dry crest of straw balanced on its spine.

A newborn lamb hauls itself upright on all four legs and sways, steam lifting off its coat in dark damp curls still faintly yellow at the tips, its ears outsized and folded over at the point, its twin still flat and folded on the straw beside the ewe's hind legs.

A damp lamb stands swaying on legs plainly too long for it, steam rising off its back, its coat in dark stuck-flat curls, and pushes its muzzle into its mother's flank while its twin is still down in the straw, ears folded, coat wet, body folded small against her side.

Two lambs sit upright in the cardboard box under the lamp, their heads and outsized ears showing over the rim, the lamp's light landing full on the tight curls at the tops of their heads and on the straw packed around them, the rest of the pen in plain quiet shadow.

The shepherd sets a wooden crate down in the pen corner and two lambs immediately prop their front feet on the rim and peer over it at each other, their enormous ears flopping forward, the lamp on its hooked flex throwing its light squarely onto the straw inside and onto their curled foreheads.

Three lambs crowd the rim of the box under the lamp, two with their chins hooked over the edge and one with its whole head inside, the lamp's light landing on their backs and on the clean straw below, a halter looped on the hurdle post beside them swinging from the disturbance.

Fifteen lambs go flat out across wet grass for no reason at all, spread wide and ragged, and wheel hard at the stone wall, one already peeled off sideways on its own heading in a completely different direction, the nearest pair's backs not clearing the bottom rail of the field gate.

A loose mob of eleven lambs pours through the gateway in a rush, the first one stopping dead in the open gap with the rest piling into its back end and banking up behind it, none of them clearing the height of the gate's second rail, the wet grass ahead untouched.

Twelve lambs wheel as one across the wet field and then immediately scatter with no plan, three of them bunching at the far wall, one peeled off and bouncing alone with all four feet leaving the ground, the rest spreading wide, their backs nowhere near the height of the stone wall.

A mob of fifteen lambs comes through the gateway in a surge while the ewes shout from behind the gate, the lambs spreading unevenly across the wet grass the moment they clear the post, the last one through stumbling on the muddy sill and correcting without slowing, already running.

A lamb stands square on its sleeping mother's back because she is the warmest flat surface in the pen, its four legs planted wide, while two more lambs are folded against her ribs on the straw, all three of them together covering less of her than her own fleece does.

Four lambs sleep piled on top of one another in a pressed hollow in the straw exactly their combined shape, the top one flat on its back with its legs up, the lowest one's ear the only part of it visible, a bucket with a handle mended with wire hanging on the hurdle post above them.

Two lambs sleep back to back in a hollow in the grass that fits them precisely, a dry crest of straw still balanced on one lamb's back from the shed, and a third lamb stands square on their sleeping mother's back because the ground is wet and she is not.

A ewe works along her two lambs nose-first in the field, pressing her muzzle into each one's flank in turn to check it, while a third lamb slides out behind her and stands at the field gate looking pleased with itself, its back barely reaching the gate's lowest rail.

A speckle-nosed ewe noses her first lamb thoroughly and then her second, turning in a tight circle to reach them both, while the third slips clear around behind her and trots off toward the wall, already several lengths away before she has finished her count.

A lamb stands on the wrong side of the hurdle entirely, having passed through a gap it cannot now locate, and presses its muzzle against the rail while its twin feeds steadily on the right side, their mother's fleece worn shiny where she has leaned on the same rail all week.
